source_note: Web-verified research on German colonial episodes: Herero-Nama genocide (Namibia 1904-08, incl. Hornkranz 1893), German East Africa (Maji-Maji, Mkwawa), Cameroon, Togo, and the human-remains acquisition networks. Key sources: SPK/Humboldt Forum provenance publications, Charité repatriation records (ArThemis), Freiburg 2014 release, German Lost Art Foundation (Kulturgutverluste/Proveana) project pages, Mission 21 archive. Structural context: an 1889 Bundesrat resolution (extended 1896) required items appropriated by German officials/military in the colonies to go to the Berlin Museum für Völkerkunde first — officer names + Berlin accessions are a systematic red-flag pattern. Corrections vs seed list: the Duala tangué was looted by Max Buchner (1884), not Kurt von Morgen; von Morgen omitted (no verified museum-supply trail). Caveats: Carl Peters and Hermann von Wissmann flagged on coercion-context and museum-association evidence rather than a specific looted-object file.

actors.name: Felix von Luschan
actors.role: Curator/director, Africa-Oceania dept., Königliches Museum für Völkerkunde Berlin; hub of colonial collecting and skull-acquisition network; Benin cataloguer
actors.region: Germany hub (Namibia, Tanzania, Cameroon, Togo, Nigeria)
actors.why_flag: Built the 'S-Sammlung' skull collection (thousands of crania from all German colonies, later Charité/SPK); solicited 'specimens' and objects from colonial officers and governors (Zürn skull, Conrau Bangwa shipments, 1898 request to Governor Puttkamer); privately acquired bones of the executed trader Hassan bin Omari Makunganya; his 'Altertümer von Benin' (1919) catalogued Berlin's 1897 loot. His name in a chain signals acquisition via colonial-military networks.
actors.source: SPK press release 22.04.2026 (West Africa skulls) — https://www.preussischer-kulturbesitz.de/pressemitteilung/artikel/2026/04/22/ ; SMB em||power||relations booklet — https://www.smb.museum/fileadmin/website/Orte/Humboldtforum/Provenienzforschung/power_relations_provenance_research_at_the_Humboldt_Forum.pdf

actors.name: Ralph Zürn
actors.role: Schutztruppe lieutenant, Okahandja (GSWA)
actors.why_flag: Ordered exhumation of Herero skulls from Okahandja graves (1903); brought a Herero skull to Germany and donated it to von Luschan; advised that concentration camps were good 'sources of specimens'.

actors.name: Lothar von Trotha
actors.role: Commander-in-chief, GSWA 1904-05; issuer of the extermination orders
actors.why_flag: Directed the genocidal war (Waterberg 1904, Omaheke, extermination proclamations); his written/photographic estate documents the campaign. Objects, photographs or remains associated with his command or estate warrant review.

actors.name: Eugen Fischer
actors.role: Anthropologist/eugenicist; Freiburg professor; researched in GSWA 1908
actors.why_flag: Travelled to GSWA in 1908 and brought skulls back to Freiburg; Herero/Nama skulls entered the Alexander Ecker Collection during his professorship; conducted race research on prisoners' remains. Freiburg repatriated 14 Namibian skulls in 2014.

actors.name: Hugo Bofinger
actors.role: Camp physician, Shark Island concentration camp
actors.why_flag: Decapitated bodies of prisoners (incl. a child), preserved heads and shipped them to Berlin institutions; conducted experiments on prisoners. Remains passing through his hands are genocide-context remains.

actors.name: Leonhard Schultze-Jena
actors.role: Zoologist/anthropologist travelling in GSWA during the 1904-08 war
actors.why_flag: By his own account took 'body parts from fresh native corpses' of killed/executed Nama during the genocide and used prisoners for collecting; material went to German university collections.

actors.name: Christian Fetzer
actors.role: Medical researcher (racial-anatomy studies on Shark Island victims)
actors.why_flag: Performed racial-anatomical studies on 17 heads of Nama who died at Shark Island (decapitated 1906 and shipped to Germany); marker for the Shark Island remains stream.

actors.name: Paul Bartels
actors.role: Berlin anatomist; recipient of Shark Island heads
actors.why_flag: Heads of prisoners who died at Shark Island (1905-07) were decapitated on site and sent to Bartels; part of the Charité collections repatriated to Namibia in 2011.

actors.name: Hans Virchow
actors.role: Berlin anatomist (Charité); recipient of gifted Herero skulls
actors.why_flag: Received two Herero skulls as gifts from collector Arthur von Gwinner; among the Charité holdings repatriated in 2011. Signals the Berlin anatomical acquisition network.

actors.name: Arthur von Gwinner
actors.role: Collector/donor of Herero skulls to Berlin anatomists
actors.why_flag: Documented as the donor of two Herero skulls (gifts to Hans Virchow) later repatriated by the Charité in 2011.

actors.name: Waldemar Belck
actors.role: Scientist on the second Lüderitz expedition (1884-85); grave robber
actors.why_flag: Looted three human skeletons from a grave during the occupation of the colony; Rudolf Virchow presented them to the Berlin Society for Anthropology in 1885 — earliest documented Namibian remains stream to Berlin.

actors.name: Rudolf Virchow
actors.role: Pathologist; founder-figure of the BGAEU; assembler of the Rudolf Virchow Collection
actors.why_flag: Presented colonial-loot remains (e.g., Belck's Namibian skeletons, 1885) to the BGAEU, whose Rudolf Virchow Collection contains numerous human remains from colonial contexts of injustice. Remains with Virchow/BGAEU provenance warrant review.
actors.source: Human Remains and Violence 4:2 (2018); 'We Want Them Back' report — https://www.bcp.fu-berlin.de/biologie/ethik-tool-box/menschliche-Gebeine---zeilenbasiert/Provenienz-101/Links-und-Downloads/We-Want-Them-Back_english-web.pdf

actors.name: Curt von François
actors.role: Schutztruppe commander, GSWA; led the raid on Hornkranz (12 April 1893)
actors.why_flag: Commanded the surprise attack that killed ~80-90 Witbooi people; Hornkranz was plundered and burned; loot included Hendrik Witbooi's Bible and whip (Linden-Museum, returned 2019). Objects from the raid trace to his command.

actors.name: Hugo von François
actors.role: Schutztruppe officer at the Hornkranz raid
actors.why_flag: Named officer in the 1893 Hornkranz attack and plunder; material attributed to him from this context warrants review.

actors.name: Kurd Schwabe
actors.role: Schutztruppe officer (Hornkranz raid participant)
actors.why_flag: Named participant officer in the Hornkranz attack and plunder (1893); veteran of both SWA wars; associated material warrants review.

actors.name: Tom von Prince
actors.role: Schutztruppe officer, German East Africa; led the storming of Mkwawa's fortress Kalenga (1894)
actors.why_flag: Stormed and looted Kalenga (stores of ivory taken; personal trophies incl. a tooth of Chief Mkwawa kept in the family). Hehe war material tied to him warrants review.

actors.name: Hermann von Wissmann
actors.role: Reichskommissar/governor of German East Africa; commander of the suppression of the Abushiri uprising 1889-90
actors.why_flag: Explorer-officer whose expeditions and command are associated with objects now in the Ethnologisches Museum Berlin; violent conquest context of his commissariat makes Wissmann-provenance material a review signal. CAVEAT: flagged on coercion-context and museum-association evidence, not a specific looted-object file.

actors.name: Carl Peters
actors.role: Founder, Society for German Colonization/DOAG; coercive treaty expeditions 1884; station chief (dismissed for atrocities)
actors.why_flag: Primary sources document coercive treaty-making, punitive raids, plunder and executions (incl. the hangings that led to his 1897 dismissal); objects with Peters provenance derive from a coercive context. CAVEAT: coercion-context evidence rather than a specific looted-object file.

actors.name: Johannes Weißenborn
actors.role: Head of ethnography, Übersee-Museum Bremen (recipient-side curator)
actors.why_flag: Actively solicited 'the most extensive selection possible' from an announced shipment of Maji-Maji 'war loot' from Dar es Salaam (arrived January 1908); marker for Bremen's trophy-colonialism intake.

actors.name: Hans Glauning
actors.role: Schutztruppe officer (German East Africa, then station chief Bamenda, Cameroon)
actors.why_flag: Donated confiscated belongings of the executed trader Hassan bin Omari Makunganya to Berlin (1896); as Bamenda commander waged permanent warfare in the Grassfields and sent ~740 inventory numbers to the Ethnologisches Museum Berlin (1901-08). Subject of a dedicated German Lost Art Foundation provenance project.

actors.name: Hans Dominik
actors.role: Schutztruppe officer, Yaoundé station chief, Cameroon; led numerous punitive expeditions
actors.why_flag: Notorious campaign commander (e.g., against the Maka from 1905, with skulls of executed people sent to Germany); his Cameroon collections in German museums are under systematic provenance research on suspicion of unlawful/coercive acquisition; described as source of 'war trophies' in SPK cellars.

actors.name: Richard Hirtler
actors.role: Colonial-era collector, Cameroon
actors.why_flag: His Cameroon collections are named alongside Glauning's and Dominik's in a German Lost Art Foundation project investigating suspected unlawful or questionable acquisition contexts.

actors.name: Gustav Conrau
actors.role: Trader, labour recruiter and collector for the Berlin Museum für Völkerkunde (Bangwa area)
actors.why_flag: Sent three paid shipments of Bangwa objects to von Luschan (1898-99), incl. the 'Bangwa Queen' (lefem figure); royal descendants dispute the 'gift' framing; his death triggered punitive expeditions (1899/1900) in which the Bangwa palace was burned and heritage looted. Bangwa objects with Conrau provenance are contested.

actors.name: Jesko von Puttkamer
actors.role: Governor of Kamerun 1895-1907
actors.why_flag: Governor during atrocity-marked campaigns; in 1898 asked by von Luschan to supply anthropological 'specimens' (incl. human remains) from the colony; Proveana-listed colonial actor. Objects/remains routed via his administration warrant review.

actors.name: Curt von Morgen
actors.role: Colonial officer, Cameroon expeditions 1889-93
actors.why_flag: SEED-LIST CORRECTION ENTRY: expeditions documented, but no fetched source verified him as a museum-collection supplier, and the Duala tangué attribution belongs to Max Buchner. Retained only as a lead requiring further verification — do not add to matching lists.

actors.name: Max von Stetten
actors.role: Commander of the Cameroon police troop, then Schutztruppe (1891-95)
actors.why_flag: Transferred 204 objects to the Munich Museum Fünf Kontinente (1893-96); the provenance project found 49 objects, incl. the 'Blue Rider Post' and Wute items, were acquired with high probability in the context of warfare/punitive expeditions he led.

actors.name: Georg August Zenker
actors.role: Botanist; head of the Jaunde (Yaoundé) station 1889-95; then private commercial collector
actors.why_flag: Sent 650+ ethnological objects (plus natural-history specimens and remains-adjacent material) to Berlin museums from a colonial-station context; a standard name in Cameroon provenance chains requiring review.

actors.name: Hans Caspar Gans Edler Herr zu Putlitz
aliases: Putlitz, Hans Caspar Gans Edler Herr zu
actors.role: Colonial officer; collector of Bamum objects
actors.why_flag: Sent 55 Bamum objects to the Ethnologisches Museum Berlin during the 1905-13 acquisition wave from Bamum, a period structured by colonial power asymmetry.

actors.name: Jakob Keller
actors.role: Basel Mission missionary in Cameroon
actors.why_flag: In 1897, with local converts, seized countless ritual objects by force ('an actual robbery' per Mission 21's own archive research), burning some and sending others to Basel; Basel Mission-provenance Cameroon objects warrant review.

actors.name: Adolf Bastian
actors.role: Founding director, Königliches Museum für Völkerkunde Berlin
actors.why_flag: Established the network of dealers, collectors, colonial officers and officials through which Cameroon and other colonial objects flowed to Berlin; research on the African holdings found most objects unlawfully acquired (booty from punitive expeditions or intimidation).

actors.name: Hans Gruner
actors.role: Head of Misahöhe station, Togo; scientist-administrator and collector
actors.why_flag: One of eight actors 'directly or indirectly involved in the colonial system' who supplied the colonial-era Togo collections (700 inventory numbers) researched at Dresden/Leipzig; acquisition tied to annexation expeditions and wars of conquest (Togo-Hinterland expedition 1894-95).

actors.name: Valentin von Massow
actors.role: Officer commanding German military expeditions in Togo (1890s)
actors.why_flag: Named actor in the Dresden/Leipzig Togo provenance project; commanded the military expedition against the Dagomba (1896); estate auctions in Lomé (1899/1900) dispersed his acquisitions.

actors.name: Gaston Thierry
actors.role: Colonial officer/station head, Togo and northern territories
actors.why_flag: Named actor in the Dresden/Leipzig Togo provenance project (collections tied to the colonial context of injustice, 1884-1914); Proveana tags include ethnographica trade.

actors.name: Adam Mischlich
actors.role: Missionary-turned-colonial official, Togo; collector-dealer
actors.why_flag: Named actor in the Dresden/Leipzig Togo provenance project; supplied Togo objects to Saxon museums 1899-1939 within the colonial context of injustice; Proveana tags include ethnographica trade.

actors.name: Adolf Diehl
actors.role: Trader/collector connected to Togo and Cameroon collections
actors.why_flag: Named actor in the Dresden/Leipzig Togo provenance project; documented as obtaining items from soldiers and officers who had taken part in colonial wars and punitive expeditions.

actors.name: Ernst F. Gütschow
actors.role: Collector/donor named in colonial Togo collections
actors.why_flag: One of the eight named actors who transferred colonial-era Togo objects to the Dresden and Leipzig ethnographic museums (1899-1939).

actors.name: Oskar Marx (Togo)
actors.role: Colonial actor named in Togo collections
actors.why_flag: One of the eight named actors in the Dresden/Leipzig Togo provenance project; collections tied to the colonial context of injustice. (Proveana full name: Ferdinand Oskar Marx.)

actors.name: Harry Grunitzky
actors.role: Military/trader collector (Togo)
actors.why_flag: One of the eight named actors in the Dresden/Leipzig Togo provenance project; collections tied to the colonial context of injustice.

actors.name: Carl Spiess
actors.role: Missionary, Norddeutsche Missionsgesellschaft (Togo/Gold Coast 1892-1914)
actors.why_flag: Collected ~500 objects — at least half sensitive/sacred Ewe items (often surrendered as 'tokens of conversion') — and transferred them to the Übersee-Museum Bremen; acquisition embedded in colonization/missionization, now under joint German-Ghanaian-Togolese research.

channels.name: J.F.G. Umlauff (Hamburg)
channels.type: natural-history and ethnographica trading house (1868-1974), incl. human remains
channels.why_flag: Leading European dealer that commissioned captains, colonial personnel and travellers to procure ethnographica and human remains via Hamburg's colonial shipping; wholesaled expedition hauls to museums worldwide (incl. 1,827 Frobenius Kasai objects to the AMNH, 1912; Benin objects to MARKK 1900-1937). Umlauff invoices/labels in a provenance chain signal colonial-trade acquisition needing review.

channels.name: Carl Hagenbeck (firm)
channels.type: animal-trading and Völkerschau enterprise with ethnographica trade
channels.why_flag: The Hagenbeck animal trade was deeply entangled with the trade in ethnographica and in people for 'Völkerschauen'; agents collected objects for the firm. Hagenbeck provenance signals show-business/colonial-trade acquisition contexts.

channels.name: Arthur Speyer (dealer dynasty, Berlin)
channels.why_flag: Among the most important German-language ethnographica dealers of the 1920s-30s; Digital Benin provenance actor (id 804); brokered exchanges with the Ethnologisches Museum Berlin and Linden-Museum, redistributing colonial-era African material (incl. Cameroon) across museums — Speyer provenance obscures original acquisition contexts.
channels.source: Digital Benin — https://digitalbenin.org/provenance/804 ; Freiburg online collection — https://onlinesammlung.freiburg.de/en/person/Speyer

channels.name: Julius Konietzko (firm, Hamburg)
channels.type: ethnographica dealership (c. 1910s onward; continued by Lore Kegel and Boris Kegel-Konietzko)
channels.why_flag: Hamburg port-based dealer supplying thousands of objects to the Museum für Völkerkunde Hamburg (MARKK) and others via intermediary networks; documented problematic acquisitions incl. a 1930 sale with punitive-expedition provenance claim (Bamenda 1911). CAVEAT: mainly a secondary-market channel for colonial-era material rather than a colonial-period looter.

channels.name: Reiche & Ruhe (Alfeld animal-trading firms)
channels.type: animal-trading companies circulating animals, people and ethnographica
channels.why_flag: PAESE provenance research documents their global networks moving ethnographica alongside animals and Völkerschau recruitment; same entangled colonial trade as Hagenbeck.

channels.name: Norddeutsche Missionsgesellschaft (Bremen Mission)
channels.type: mission society collection channel (Togo/Gold Coast → Übersee-Museum Bremen)
channels.why_flag: Missionaries (esp. Carl Spiess, 1892-1914) transferred ~500 Ewe objects, many sacred, obtained within the coercive frame of colonization and missionization; mission-society provenance for Togo/Ghana objects warrants review.

channels.name: Basel Mission
channels.type: mission society collection channel (Cameroon, Ghana → Museum der Kulturen Basel)
channels.why_flag: Its Cameroon collection includes objects taken by force (documented 1897 seizure of ritual objects by missionary Jakob Keller); Basel Mission provenance for Cameroon Grassfields material is a review signal.

channels.name: Charité anatomical collections (Berlin)
channels.why_flag: Held remains of Herero and Nama genocide victims among ~7,000-7,700 skulls; repatriations to Namibia 2011, 2014, 2018 after the Charité Human Remains Project; residual holdings transferred to SPK in 2011. Charité provenance = genocide-era acquisition risk.

channels.name: Luschan S-Sammlung (Berlin, now SPK)
channels.type: anthropological skull collection (c. 1900, all German colonies)
channels.why_flag: Core of the ~7,700 skulls SPK took over from the Charité in 2011; West Africa portion (574 examined, 2026) includes skulls of Cameroonian railway workers, robbed necropolises, battlefields and executions; East Africa portion (~1,100) researched 2023. S-Sammlung numbers in a chain are a strong red flag.

channels.name: Luschan private collection (sold to AMNH, 1924)
channels.why_flag: Luschan's personal collection — assembled through the same colonial networks — was sold by his widow to the American Museum of Natural History in 1924 and remains there; AMNH 'Luschan' provenance can conceal German-colonial acquisition contexts.

channels.name: Alexander Ecker Collection (Freiburg)
channels.why_flag: Contained skulls labelled 'Herero' and 'Hottentot' most likely added via Eugen Fischer's 1908 GSWA research; 14 Namibian skulls repatriated in 2014. Ecker Collection provenance for African remains warrants review.

channels.name: BGAEU Rudolf Virchow Collection
aliases: Berliner Gesellschaft für Anthropologie, Ethnologie und Urgeschichte
channels.why_flag: Contains numerous human remains from colonial contexts of injustice, incl. Namibian remains received from 1885 (Belck/Virchow); BGAEU/Virchow provenance is a review signal for African remains.

channels.name: Schutztruppe (German colonial forces)
channels.why_flag: The organizational frame for punitive-expedition looting across GSWA, GEA and Cameroon; under the 1889/1896 Bundesrat rules, officer acquisitions flowed to Berlin. Schutztruppe-officer provenance is a systematic review signal. GENERIC term — flat matching only via officer names, not the word itself.
